explanation: Both queries join table3 (T1) to table2 (T2) and return the most recent T1.c6 among joined rows after filtering on T2.c36. Q2 correctly filters with NOT IN ('-','+-'). Q1’s WHERE clause is malformed: WHERE T2.c36 <> '-' OR '+-' is parsed as (T2.c36 <> '-') OR ('+-'). In many engines this either reduces to T2.c36 <> '-' (string literal coerced to FALSE) or becomes always TRUE (if non-empty strings are truthy). In either case, Q1 does not exclude '+-' the way Q2 does (and may even fail to exclude '-' entirely), so Q1 can keep rows that Q2 filters out.
counterexample_dsp: Make the T1 row with the greatest c6 join only to T2 rows where c36 = '+-'. Then Q2 (NOT IN ('-','+-')) filters those out, while Q1 (effectively c36 <> '-' due to the OR '+-' literal) keeps them. Add another T1 with a smaller c6 that joins to a T2 row with c36 not in the forbidden set so Q2 returns that smaller date.
